This page goes with **Chapter 4, Basics of Rhythm** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/BasicsOfRhythm.html).

**You already know this.** You move to macrobeats and microbeats, chant rhythm patterns on **du de** (usual duple) and **du da di**
(usual triple) (Gordon 86, 105), and read and write those patterns. This chapter gives the textbook's **names** for the symbols you
already read. Gordon's warning applies: a player who only knows the time-value names "resort[s] to counting", and the tempo and meter
suffer (Gordon 38). So keep chanting: the names are for talking about the notation, not for performing from it.

Press ▶ to hear an example. Click any heading to fold its section.

## What you know → what the book calls it

| You say (MLT) | The book says (Hutchinson ch. 4) |
|---|---|
| macrobeat | the beat (in simple meter); the dotted beat (in compound meter) |
| microbeat | the division of the beat |
| du, de, du da di, ta | note values: quarter, eighth, sixteenth … |
| an elongation (a note longer than a microbeat) | a longer value, a dotted note, or a tie |
| usual duple / usual triple | simple / compound meter (see [Meter: Two Ways](meter-taxonomy.qmd)) |
| a triple division inside duple meter (usual combined) | a triplet (a tuplet) |
| the measure signature | the time signature |

## 4.1 and 4.4 Time signatures and meter

The book reads the time signature as two numbers: how many beats in a bar, and what kind of note gets the beat.
[Read 4.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/TimeSignature.html) ·
[Read 4.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/meter.html)

The two systems sort meters differently, and this is the one place in the chapter where they disagree. The full comparison is on
[Meter: Two Ways to Sort Time Signatures](meter-taxonomy.qmd). The short version:

- **Simple** meter (2/4, 3/4, 4/4): each beat divides in **2**. You chant it **du de**: usual duple.
- **Compound** meter (6/8, 9/8, 12/8): each beat divides in **3**. You chant it **du da di**: usual triple.
- The book's *duple / triple / quadruple* counts **beats in a bar**. Your *duple / triple* names **how each beat divides**. So 6/8 is
  "compound duple" in the book and "usual triple" to you (Gordon 176).

## 4.2 Note values: naming what you chant

Here is one bar of usual duple in 2/4 and one of usual triple in 6/8, with your syllables under the notes.
[Read 4.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DurationalSymbols.html)

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80" data-sing="off"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Usual duple in 2/4
M:2/4
L:1/16
K:C
B4 B4 | B2B2 B2B2 | BBBB BBBB | B8 |]
w:du du du de du de du ta de ta du ta de ta du
</script></div>

| In 2/4 you chant | The book's name | US / UK name |
|---|---|---|
| du (a macrobeat) | quarter note, the beat | quarter / crotchet |
| du de (two microbeats) | two eighth notes | eighth / quaver |
| du ta de ta | four sixteenth notes | sixteenth / semiquaver |
| du held through two macrobeats | half note | half / minim |

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="60" data-sing="off"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Usual triple in 6/8
M:6/8
L:1/8
K:C
B3 B3 | BBB BBB | B2B B2B | B6 |]
w:du du du da di du da di du di du di du
</script></div>

| In 6/8 you chant | The book's name |
|---|---|
| du (a macrobeat) | dotted quarter note, the beat |
| du da di | three eighth notes |
| du … di (long-short) | quarter then eighth |
| du held through two macrobeats | dotted half note |

**The thing to notice:** in 2/4 the macrobeat is a quarter note; in 6/8 it is a **dotted** quarter. That is why compound meters need
dots: a plain note can't be split evenly into three.

## 4.3 Dots and ties: names for elongations

A note longer than a microbeat is an **elongation**. You already read them. The book has two ways to write them.
[Read 4.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DotsAndTies.html)

- A **dot** adds half the note's value. In 2/4, a dotted quarter + eighth is the pattern you chant **du — de**, held through the first
  microbeat of the next beat.
- A **tie** joins two notes into one sound. Use it when the sound crosses a barline, or a beat the reader needs to see.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80" data-sing="off"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Dotted quarter + eighth, then the same with a tie
M:2/4
L:1/8
K:C
B3 B | B2 B2 | B2- B B | B4 |]
w:du de du du du _ de du
</script></div>

## 4.5 Tuplets: usual combined

When a duple beat is split into three, you chant **du da di** inside usual duple: Gordon calls the mix **usual combined** (Gordon
175–176). The book writes it as a **triplet**, with a 3 over the notes.
[Read 4.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Tuplets.html)

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="72" data-sing="off"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Du de, then a triplet: du da di
M:2/4
L:1/8
K:C
B B (3BBB | B B (3BBB | B2 B2 |]
w:du de du da di du de du da di du du
</script></div>

## 4.6 Writing rhythms the reader can audiate

The book's list of common errors is mostly one rule: **show the beat**. Beam notes so each macrobeat's microbeats are grouped together,
and tie across the middle of the bar rather than hiding it inside one long note. If you can see where each **du** falls, you can
chant it at sight.
[Read 4.6](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/CommonRhythmicNotationErrors.html)

## Bridging: from syllables to names

1. **Chant first.** Chant the pattern on du de or du da di, moving to the macrobeats.
2. **Find du.** Every du is a macrobeat. Say which note value it is: quarter in 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4; dotted quarter in 6/8.
3. **Name the rest from du.** A de is half of it, a ta a quarter of it. A note held through a du is an elongation: name it as a longer
   note, a dot or a tie.
4. **Go the other way.** Given "write four eighths and a half note in 2/4", chant it first (du de du de | du), then write it.

## Check yourself

1. In 3/4, what note value is du?
2. In 6/8, you chant du da di. What are the three notes called?
3. In 2/4, you chant du ta de ta. Name the notes.
4. What does the book call usual combined meter's triple division inside a duple beat?
5. Why does 6/8 need a dotted quarter for its beat?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. A quarter note.
2. Eighth notes.
3. Four sixteenth notes.
4. A triplet (a kind of tuplet).
5. Its beat divides in three eighths; only a dotted quarter lasts three eighths.
:::

Practise reading and chanting with [Rhythm Patterns](../practice/rhythms.qmd). Related: [Major Scales and Key Signatures](major-scales.qmd).
